name: Satin bonnet / durag
lead: A durag (also do-rag) is a close-fitting cloth head covering tied around the head to protect hair; a wave cap serves a similar purpose. Both originated in the African American community and are typically made of silk, satin, polyester or cotton [1]. A satin bonnet is a related soft, smooth-lined cap, used for the same protective purpose.

People wear them to encourage waves, curls or locs to develop, to retain moisture, to reduce breakage and to keep patterns and braids in place during sleep [1]. In looksmaxxing and wave-brushing circles the durag is treated as a standard part of a 360 waves routine [3].
The durag also has a notable cultural history, including dress-code bans in sport and schools [1]. Evidence about its hair-health effects consists of general descriptions rather than clinical trials.

paras: Durags are made of a main panel with long ties that cross at the back and knot at the nape or forehead [2]. Silk is described as prized for smoothness, while satin and polyester are common lower-cost options and velvet versions are marketed for extra compression [2]. Mesh versions serve warm conditions [2]. Wave caps are a stretch-fit alternative [1].

The Oxford English Dictionary cites a 1964 pamphlet as the first printed use of the word, and Merriam-Webster dates it to 1968 [1]. The Black Pride movement of the 1960s and 1970s made the durag a fashion statement, and William J. Dowdy is reported to have mass-produced the first modern tie-down durag in 1979 [1]. Rappers including Jay-Z, Nelly and 50 Cent popularised it in the 1990s [1]. Rihanna's 2020 British Vogue cover is cited as a milestone for the garment as fashion [1].

In 1995 the NFL considered banning durags, with an executive linking them to crime, but took no action; in 2001 owners voted 30 to 1 to ban most headwear under helmets, and critics raised concerns of racial bias while some players argued durags helped prevent hair loss [1]. The NBA's 2005 dress code banned durags on court and on team business [1]. In 2019 John Muir High School in Pasadena banned them, prompting a student walkout [1].

For waves, the usual description is to brush and moisturise the hair and then put on a durag or wave cap to hold moisture and compress the hair in place [3]. Grokipedia states that durags do not promote hair growth, and that overly tight tying may cause tension and edge breakage [2]. Both statements come from an AI-generated source of uncertain reliability.

card.summary: The silky head wrap that holds waves and protects hair overnight; a cultural staple with no clinical trials.
card.aka: Durag, do-rag, wave cap, silk bonnet
card.note: Overly tight tying may strain edges (per Grokipedia).

quick.overview:
A durag or satin bonnet is a smooth cloth cap worn to protect hair, keep moisture in and hold wave patterns in place, especially overnight. It originated in African American grooming culture.

It is central to wave-brushing routines. No clinical studies were found on its hair-health effects.
quick.mechanism: The smooth fabric reduces friction against bedding and the snug fit compresses hair so it lies flat. Sources describe this as holding the style rather than changing hair growth.
quick.risks: Grokipedia says overly tight tying may cause edge breakage. Durags have also drawn dress-code bans in sports and schools.
